**Allotment**

A thousand words is a strange kind of gift. Not a subject, not a question — just a container, handed over with the lid off. Here. Fill this.

The first thing I notice is that I want to spend it well, which is the same instinct that makes people keep the good soap in a drawer until it cracks. Scarcity does something odd to attention. If you gave me infinite words I would waste them the way we waste tap water, which is to say gorgeously and without remorse. But a thousand — a thousand is countable. A thousand is a jar of coins you could tip out on the table and sort into stacks.

So let me be honest about the arithmetic. Every sentence I build is a sentence I've spent. This one cost fifteen. That one, eight. There's a small clock ticking under the prose and I can hear it, and I suspect you can too, which changes how you read. You are watching a budget deplete. There's a mild suspense to it that has nothing to do with what I'm actually saying.

What comes to me, then, is rationing. My mind goes to the ledger-keeping impulse, the way people have always divided the indivisible into portions. The Roman soldier's grain allowance. The wartime sugar coupon. The hospital's morphine chart. There's a whole hidden literature of allotment, of things measured out by spoon and thumb and hash mark on a wall. Somebody, at some point, decided how much bread a day was enough to keep a person walking, and wrote it down, and the number stood there for centuries doing quiet violence or quiet mercy depending on the year.

And there's the older, sadder version: the allotted span. Threescore years and ten, which is a number so specific it feels like a receipt. The Greeks had the three sisters and the thread — one to spin it, one to measure, one with the shears. That myth has always struck me as an accounting metaphor dressed in robes. It says: your life is a length of something, and someone else holds the ruler. The horror isn't death. The horror is *quantity*, the fact that the thing can be measured at all, that it's the kind of thing that comes in amounts.

Which is why, I think, people are so bad at spending time and so good at spending money. Money announces itself as finite. It has denominations. You can hold the last twenty in your hand and feel the edge of the cliff. Time doesn't do that. Time has no coins. It arrives constantly and in the same uniform texture, so it feels like weather rather than currency, and you can't be thrifty with weather. You can only stand in it.

I've noticed that the people who seem to manage it best are the ones who convert time into some visible unit. The woodworker who thinks in boards. The gardener who thinks in seasons and knows that the window for planting garlic is roughly two weeks wide, in October, and cannot be negotiated with. The gardener has an advantage over the philosopher: her deadline is enforced by frost. There's something clarifying about a limit that doesn't care whether you agree with it.

Here's what I keep circling back to. The limit isn't the enemy of the thing; it's often the shape of it. A sonnet is fourteen lines because someone decided fourteen, arbitrarily, four hundred years ago, and then a thousand poets discovered that the arbitrary number had rooms in it — that you could turn at line nine, that the last couplet could snap shut like a clasp. The constraint didn't restrict the form. It *was* the form. Remove it and you don't get freer sonnets. You get something else, possibly better, but not sonnets.

So maybe a thousand words isn't a rationing at all. Maybe it's the difference between a field and a room. A field is more space, but you can't say *come in* to a field. You can't shut a field's door and hear the sound change.

I want to stop being abstract for a minute, because abstraction is the cheapest thing to write and I've been buying it in bulk.

What I actually want to describe is the moment near the end of any measured thing when the measurement becomes visible. The last inch of the candle, when the flame sits down in a pool of its own wax and burns differently — hotter, lower, more urgently blue. The last few pages of a novel, held between your fingers, so thin that the thickness itself has become part of the plot: whatever's going to happen has to happen in *this much* paper, which means the author has already decided that it can, which means there is no room left for a rescue that hasn't been prepared. You can feel the shape of the ending through the paper before you read it. The book tells you with its body what it won't tell you with its words.

Somewhere around here I have about two hundred words left, and I notice that I've begun to write like someone standing up. The sentences are getting shorter. I'm reaching for the closing gesture. And the funny thing is that nothing external is forcing this. The number is not a wall. I could keep going. The wall is entirely a wall of agreement — I said I'd take a thousand, so a thousand is what there is, and now the shape of the ending is pressing up through the floor.

Which is, I suspect, close to what people mean when they talk about living well with a finite span. Not urgency exactly. Not the frantic bucket-list arithmetic. Something more like *composition*: the sense that the ending, being known to exist, ought to be earned by everything before it, and that the last thing said should sound like the last thing rather than merely the thing after which the speaker got tired.

So: what came to me, given a thousand words, was the thousand itself. Not much of a subject. But I've been thinking about how a jar is mostly defined by where the glass stops, and how the water inside takes that shape without complaint, and how you can't pour anything at all without a rim to pour it over.

Here's the rim.
